keyVerseText: And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. Manasseh: that is, Forgetting
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun עָמָל (ʻâmâl) derives from the root עָמַל (ʻâmal), which means to labor or toil with effort and weariness. This root emphasizes strenuous work that is often burdensome or irksome, highlighting not just physical exertion but also the mental or emotional strain that accompanies it. The literal sense of ʻâmâl conveys a deep, wearing effort that surpasses simple work, encompassing suffering and hardship that affect the whole person.
usageInScripture: Throughout Scripture, ʻâmâl appears about 55 times and is translated variously as mischief, labour, toil, trouble, and sorrow. This range shows that the word covers both the experience of hard work and the distress or pain associated with it, whether physical or spiritual. The frequent use of terms like 'mischief' and 'trouble' alongside 'labour' reveals the word’s broad semantic field, encompassing personal affliction as well as the consequences of iniquity or perverseness.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ʻâmâl enriches our grasp of the biblical narrative of human struggle and redemption. It reminds believers that toil and suffering are integral parts of the fallen human condition, reflecting both the curse of sin and the trials of life. Yet, the presence of ʻâmâl also points to God’s sustaining grace amid wearisome effort and sorrow. Recognizing the depth of this term encourages faith in God’s provision and comfort, trusting that He transforms human toil into a testimony of perseverance and hope in Christ.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 41:51, Joseph names his firstborn Manasseh, saying, 'For God... hath made me forget all my toil.' Here, ʻâmâl signifies the cumulative burden of Joseph’s past hardships and labors. The use of this word underscores the profound relief and divine healing Joseph experiences, as God enables him to move beyond the painful efforts and troubles of his earlier life. This verse powerfully illustrates how God’s intervention can bring peace and restoration, turning wearisome toil into a forgotten memory through His grace.
